{"id": "16:15/q05", "question": "What is reported about the earth and mountains at creation?", "turns_on": "The accounts differ in speaker, details of the earth's movement and complaint, and the sequence of the strength exchange.", "positions": [{"id": "16:15/q05/p1", "position": "The new earth swayed; angels feared it could not support inhabitants; by morning mountains steadied it, their origin unknown to the angels.", "reasons": "The account is attributed variously to al-Ḥasan, Qays ibn ʿAbbād or ʿUbādah, and Wahb ibn Munabbih; Qatādah likewise says the earth moved before the mountain stakes. Some tellings omit either the angels' fear or ignorance of the mountains' origin. Kuranyolu summarizes older commentaries as describing an initially flat, uninhabitable earth. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Nasafī relay the account without a named transmitter."}, {"id": "16:15/q05/p2", "position": "The earth heaved and complained about carrying sinners and corpses; God anchored it with visible and unseen mountains, though it still quivered.", "reasons": "The report is attributed to ʿAlī; versions describe human sin, impurity, and the earth trembling like flesh."}, {"id": "16:15/q05/p3", "position": "The Prophet said mountains steadied the earth, followed by a sequence of stronger things ending in secret charity.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī transmits this through Anas; al-Tirmidhī grades it gharīb and says this is its only known marfūʿ route. An unattributed exchange in al-Durr instead compares water, fire, wind, man and woman."}, {"id": "16:15/q05/p4", "position": "An unattributed strength exchange places water above fire, wind above water, man above wind, and woman above man.", "reasons": "Al-Durr gives this separate chain of comparisons without an attribution."}]}

Al-Nasafī records this alongside the aversion analysis."}, {"id": "16:15/q07/p2", "position": "It means placing mountains out of dislike or fear that the earth should sway, with an omitted noun of aversion.", "reasons": "The Basran analysis supplies a causal noun before an; al-Nasafī notes noun deletion is common. {"id": "16:15/q08", "question": "What does 'rivers' refer to here?", "turns_on": "Whether the illustration uses naturally named rivers or human-benefiting canals.", "positions": [{"id": "16:15/q08/p1", "position": "The rivers God made throughout the earth, including famous named rivers.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī names the Nile, Euphrates, Tigris, Sayḥān and Jayḥān; al-Ṭabrisī adds similar rivers. Bursevī locates the Euphrates at Kufa, Tigris at Baghdad, Jayḥūn at Balkh, Jayḥān at Adana, Sīḥūn in India, Sayḥān at al-Maṣṣīṣa and Nile in Egypt. Mujāhid says every town has rivers. Bursevī calls anhar the plural of nahr, also nahar, a watercourse."}, {"id": "16:15/q08/p2", "position": "They include canals flowing through the earth for human benefit.", "reasons": "Islahi uses canals in his explanation of God's provision."}]}
{"id": "16:15/q09", "question": "How is 'and rivers' governed grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether alqā can directly govern rivers by meaning 'made,' or whether the change of object requires a supplied verb, and what that verb is.", "positions": [{"id": "16:15/q09/p1", "position": "It coordinates directly with rawāsi under alqā, understood as 'made' or 'created.'", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī cites 50:7, 41:10 and 20:39; Abū Ḥayyān cites 78:6–7 and 41:10; al-Samīn explicitly rejects Ibn ʿAṭiyyah's elided-verb parse. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah takes this ellipsis as support for a more specific alqā; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī report it but reject any claim that it is consensus. Al-Qurṭubī allows 'made in' or 'cast into'; Islahi notes recoverable wording about paths and landmarks."}, {"id": "16:15/q09/p3", "position": "The omitted verb may specifically be 'He split or carved rivers through the earth.'", "reasons": "Abū al-Baqāʾ's proposal is reported by Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn (who calls it apt) and al-Ālūsī; the latter cites a line about feeding straw and cold water to illustrate coordination of clauses."}]}
{"id": "16:15/q10", "question": "What benefits do rivers supply?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:15/q10/p1", "position": "They supply water, irrigation, provision and transport for settlements and fields.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī names directing water to gardens; Ibn Kathīr describes rivers crossing regions, deserts and mountains to inhabited lands, with differing sizes, speeds and seasons under God's measure. {"id": "16:15/q11", "question": "Why do rivers follow mountains in the verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:15/q11/p1", "position": "Most rivers begin at springs in mountains.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī attributes this to rational sciences; Abū Ḥayyān transmits him, al-Ālūsī repeats it, and Study Quran cites the pairing with 13:3 and 27:61."}]}
{"id": "16:15/q12", "question": "How do seas avoid overflowing despite river inflow?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:15/q12/p1", "position": "Seasonal heat evaporates water, which condenses into rain and replenishes rivers, balancing river inflow to the seas.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī reasons that unbalanced inflow would inundate the earth; summer solar heat remains in the ground through winter, warms waters, lifts vapor like steam from a pot, and renewed rain revives land and rivers each year."}]}
{"id": "16:15/q13", "question": "What are the subul?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:15/q13/p1", "position": "Roads, routes and passable ways across land, including passages through mountains.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī gives sabīl as the singular and compares ṭarīq/ṭuruq; Qatādah cites the usage at 20:53. Waththāb."}, {"id": "16:16/q05/p4", "position": "The plural sounding form results from deletion of the wāw of nujūm.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyyah and Rāzī report this explanation; Samin compares a shortened plural and cites Abū al-Baqāʾ's khiyām/khaym analogy. Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī prefer treating the form as an ordinary plural."}, {"id": "16:16/q05/p5", "position": "Mujāhid reads the full plural al-nujūm, retaining its wāw.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī reports this reading from Mujāhid."}]}
{"id": "16:16/q06", "question": "What does 'they find guidance' mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:16/q06/p1", "position": "They know, recognize and discern the route or direction.", "reasons": "Muqātil contrasts this with 4:98, where not finding a path means not knowing the way. {"id": "16:16/q07", "question": "For what travel or orientation do the stars guide?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause is limited to sea travel, covers journeys on both land and sea, also indicates prayer direction, or includes timekeeping; the neighboring sea passage and breadth of the blessing are cited.", "positions": [{"id": "16:16/q07/p1", "position": "They guide journeys by night on land and sea, especially where ordinary landmarks fail.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās distinguishes day markers and night stars (Ṭabarī, Ṭabrisī, Ibn Kathīr, Durr). Muqātil lists fixed stars plus mountains. Māwardī calls all journeys the majority view. Rāzī prefers land and sea as the broader blessing. Biqāʿī calls stellar guidance the clearest and most comprehensive, even by day. Bursevī stresses deserts and sea at night; Ibn ʿĀshūr stresses sailors unable to moor each night. Study Quran says guidance spans times and places. Ibn al-Jawzī transmits al-ʿAwfī from Ibn ʿAbbās on navigation by stars at night; he also reports travel guidance as one interpretation of the clause."}, {"id": "16:16/q07/p2", "position": "The star guidance is specifically for sea travel.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports some commentators infer this restriction from the preceding discussion of the sea; Durr reports Ibrāhīm's stellar guidance at sea. Rāzī prefers the wider land-and-sea application."}, {"id": "16:16/q07/p3", "position": "Stars indicate the qibla, including for travelers on land and sea.", "reasons": "Māwardī and Ṭabrisī report qibla as an alternative purpose; reports from Ibn ʿAbbās and the Prophet link al-Jady to qibla (Māwardī, Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān). Wāḥidī, Thaʿlabī and Baghawī say roads and qibla; Rāzī argues route indicators can indicate qibla too. Study Quran cites this in unfamiliar territory. Ibn al-Jawzī reports finding the direction of prayer as the other interpretation of stellar guidance."}, {"id": "16:16/q07/p4", "position": "Stars also provide a measure of time.", "reasons": "Zajjāj includes marking years and reckoning among their purposes; Islāḥī says desert travelers measure time by them."}]}
{"id": "16:16/q08", "question": "Who are 'they' in 'they are guided'?", "turns_on": "Whether the third person singles out Quraysh for their expertise or generalizes the guidance to all people; the shift of grammatical person is explained accordingly.", "positions": [{"id": "16:16/q08/p1", "position": "Quraysh, especially their trading travelers skilled in star navigation.", "reasons": "Rāzī, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, Samin, Bursevī and Study Quran cite their journeys and skill; the shift from direct address makes their obligation to reflect, thank God or affirm tawḥīd especially strong. Ālūsī reports and develops this reading. Biqāʿī includes Quraysh as the first and most knowledgeable addressees while extending the statement outward."}, {"id": "16:16/q08/p2", "position": "All travelers or earth's inhabitants, with a shift from direct address to third person.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī extends the address from Quraysh to Arabs and all inhabitants. Ālūsī reports the preceding addressees broadly. Ṭabāṭabāʾī suggests the shift avoids repeating the second-person 'you find guidance' of the prior verses."}]}

{"id": "16:16/q10", "question": "What purposes were the stars created to serve?", "turns_on": "Whether the list of divinely assigned uses is limited to three or includes calculation of years.", "positions": [{"id": "16:16/q10/p1", "position": "Adorning heaven, stoning devils, and guiding people are their three stated purposes.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā links the lamps and missiles to 67:5 and guidance to 6:97. {"id": "16:16/q11", "question": "What may people learn or claim from the stars?", "turns_on": "The distinction drawn between practical observation of routes, direction and times and forecasts claiming knowledge of future events.", "positions": [{"id": "16:16/q11/p1", "position": "Learning stars for routes, qibla and times is permissible.", "reasons": "ʿUmar permits enough astronomy for roads and qibla, then advises learning genealogy for kinship (Bursevī). {"id": "16:16/q13", "question": "How should the qibla be found when its direction is uncertain?", "turns_on": "Whether practical star bearings yield exact orientation or only an adequate general direction; the geographical objections concern changing meridians and uncertain coordinates.", "positions": [{"id": "16:16/q13/p1", "position": "Use available indications, including stars, other heavenly bodies, winds and terrestrial signs, and reason toward the likeliest direction.", "reasons": "Rāzī accepts the jurists' inference from route guidance and requires reasoning when signs appear. Ibn al-ʿArabī says ordinary people can use conspicuous fixed al-Jady and Farqads, while experts use risings, settings and north/south positions; he instructs placing the pole behind the left shoulder."}, {"id": "16:16/q13/p2", "position": "Stars and other means establish the general qibla direction, but exact determination is difficult or impossible.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Bannāʾ says a star above Mecca does not keep the same bearing in another city, al-Jady's shoulder or side rule depends on an uncertain meridian, the midsummer zenith differs between cities, and even Indian-circle methods depend on uncertain latitude and longitude. {"id": "16:16/q14", "question": "What follows if someone prays toward a wrong direction?", "turns_on": "Whether the error reflects a failure to use available signs or is discovered after carrying out the required effort.", "positions": [{"id": "16:16/q14/p1", "position": "If signs were apparent and the person failed to reason, the prayer must be repeated or is invalid.", "reasons": "Rāzī calls such error negligence and requires repetition when it becomes clear. {"id": "16:16/q15", "question": "What should one do if no qibla signs appear?", "turns_on": "Whether equal uncertainty permits selecting one direction or requires covering every possibility for certainty.", "positions": [{"id": "16:16/q15/p1", "position": "Choose any direction because none has evidence favoring it.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports this proposed rule when all directions are equal."}, {"id": "16:16/q15/p2", "position": "Pray toward every direction to discharge the duty with certainty.", "reasons": "Rāzī prefers this rule. {"id": "16:16/q16", "question": "What inward guidance is read in the star and signs?", "turns_on": "Which spiritual referents the physical signs symbolize and whether guidance is attributed directly to God or mediated through named figures.", "positions": [{"id": "16:16/q16/p1", "position": "The signs are landmarks of the path and stars of gnosis, yet God alone guides the seeker to Himself.", "reasons": "Al-Mālikī in Sulamī says no created sign or route reaches God apart from God; arrival and severance follow prior decree."}, {"id": "16:16/q16/p2", "position": "The star symbolizes the Messenger, and the signs symbolize the Imams or Ahl al-Bayt.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī transmits Abū ʿAbd Allāh's interpretation and treats it as inner meaning, supported by a report naming the Prophet the star and the Ahl al-Bayt earth's signs and protection."}]}
{"id": "16:16/q17", "question": "What wider point does this verse make in its passage?", "turns_on": "The sources draw different connected lessons from the sequence: gratitude and reasoning, exclusive worship, or the placement of spiritual guidance.", "positions": [{"id": "16:16/q17/p1", "position": "Created navigational aids are among God's blessings and call people to reflection and gratitude.", "reasons": "Jishumī groups them with animals, trees and fruits and says reflection makes reasoning obligatory rather than uncritical imitation. Ibn ʿĀshūr sees evidence in beneficial creatures on Earth's surface; Asad says the passage returns to human intellectual potential, linking 16:4, 16:8, 16:14 and 2:30-33. Study Quran stresses guidance across time and place. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the earlier 'casting' images additions to a complete earth: mountains from seismic disturbance or perhaps celestial debris, rivers from rain, and roads/markers later; he cites analogous extension of 'casting' at 54:25."}, {"id": "16:16/q17/p2", "position": "Because these blessings are created by God, worship belongs to Him rather than deities that created none.", "reasons": "Islāḥī draws this implication from the created benefits; Ālūsī likewise links Quraysh's debt of thanks with tawḥīd."}, {"id": "16:16/q17/p3", "position": "The placement of the spiritual-guidance verse avoids confusion and apparent contradiction with physical navigation signs.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī says a later placement after the physical signs might seem more natural but the present placement has this clarifying effect."}]}
{"id": "16:16/q18", "question": "What does the Arabic case contrast show about settled distinguishing traits?", "turns_on": "Whether the quality is established as a distinguishing mark or observed as an ongoing act.", "positions": [{"id": "16:16/q18/p1", "position": "Rafʿ presents knowledge and similar qualities as established virtues or distinguishing marks.", "reasons": "Sībawayh uses lahu ʿilm ʿilm al-fuqahāʾ with ḥilm, ʿaql and faḍl; lahu sharaf/dīn/fahm likewise describes stable qualities, while yatedayyan, yatasharraf and yatafahham describe unfinished ones."}, {"id": "16:16/q18/p2", "position": "The accusative presents an action or quality observed while occurring, before it is settled.", "reasons": "Sībawayh contrasts accusative ʿilm for someone encountered while learning with praise for established knowledge; lahu ṣawt ṣawt ḥimār describes the sound made then, since sound is an action rather than a settled bodily trait."}]}

{"id": "16:16/q21", "question": "What signs of permission or prohibition are discussed with divine benefits?", "turns_on": "The legal force of permission language, divine rebuke, mention of a favor, and a speaker's expression of personal avoidance.", "positions": [{"id": "16:16/q21/p1", "position": "Permission can be inferred from explicit allowance, removed blame, pardon, benefit, silence, or approval during revelation.", "reasons": "Burhān lists permission, conditional choice and other forms, mentions 16:5, and cites Jābir's report of withdrawal while Quran was revealed and Ḥassān's poetry before the Prophet as tacit approvals."}, {"id": "16:16/q21/p2", "position": "Divine rebuke before an act signals its prohibition.", "reasons": "Burhān cites rebukes in al-Anfāl, al-Tawba, al-Aḥzāb, al-Taḥrīm and ʿAbasa and discusses Ibn ʿAbd al-Salām's treatment of rebuke."}, {"id": "16:16/q21/p3", "position": "God cannot present a forbidden thing as a favor.", "reasons": "Burhān rejects explaining the favor as merely creating ability to endure it."}, {"id": "16:16/q21/p4", "position": "A speaker's 'As for me, I do not do it' expresses dislike.", "reasons": "Burhān cites the Prophet's statement that he does not eat reclining."}]}
{"id": "16:36/q01", "question": "What does ummah mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the word marks a human group, a span of time, or both.", "positions": [{"id": "16:36/q01/p1", "position": "A human community or people, broadly understood.", "reasons": "Asad allows a civilization embracing both people and period; Kuranyolu defines a large group united by ancestry, traits, interests, ideals, religion, time or homeland, notes its plural umam and its narrower religious use for a prophet's followers, and prefers the broad sense here, citing 2:128, 2:134, 2:213, 11:118–119."}, {"id": "16:36/q01/p2", "position": "A period of time, so the sending occurred at every period.", "reasons": "Asad offers this as an alternative rendering of ummah."}]}
{"id": "16:36/q02", "question": "How universal was the sending of messengers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:36/q02/p1", "position": "God sent a messenger to every community or generation, including the present community.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Tabari, Zajjaj, Jishumi, and others state the universal practice; Wahidi, Baghawi, Tabrisi, Ibn al-Jawzi, and Bursevi compare Muhammad's mission to earlier missions. Tabatabai ties universality to human need and 16:35; Study Quran cites 10:47, 35:23, 67:9 and notes witnesses and books in 4:41, 16:84, 28:75, 45:28. {"id": "16:36/q03", "question": "What did every messenger call people to do?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:36/q03/p1", "position": "Worship God alone, affirm His oneness, and shun false worship.", "reasons": "Tabari adds exclusive obedience and sincere devotion; Jishumi says prophets begin with monotheism and justice, urge reflection on proofs, then teach laws because laws depend on those foundations. {"id": "16:36/q04", "question": "How does an introduce the command?", "turns_on": "Whether an explains the speech implied by sending or forms a verbal noun governed by an understood preposition.", "positions": [{"id": "16:36/q04/p1", "position": "It is explanatory: sending a messenger implies a spoken message or command.", "reasons": "Tabrisi, Bursevi, Ibn Ashur, and Alusi derive the explanatory force from the verbal or command sense of sending; Samin records this parse. {"id": "16:36/q05", "question": "What inward sense does worship or the call receive?", "turns_on": "The distinct inward emphases are worship as the knower's servanthood and the prophetic call's disciplining of desire.", "positions": [{"id": "16:36/q05/p1", "position": "Worship adorns knowers, whose best state is service and surrender of personal claims for what is due to God.", "reasons": "Tustari states the reading; Sulami reports it from Sahl in nearly the same terms."}, {"id": "16:36/q05/p2", "position": "Prophets call to divine oneness and servanthood and away from natural impulses, desires, and passions.", "reasons": "Sulami transmits this from Muhammad ibn al-Fadl."}]}
{"id": "16:36/q06", "question": "What is the taghut to be avoided?", "turns_on": "Whether taghut names all illicit objects of worship, misleading agents, Satan in particular, or idols in particular; several broad definitions include the narrower cases.", "positions": [{"id": "16:36/q06/p1", "position": "Anything worshipped besides God, including idols, people, or Satan.", "reasons": "Thalabi, Baghawi, Ibn Atiyya, Razi, Qurṭubi and others state the general sense; Ibn Atiyya includes a consenting human, stone or wood; Ibn Qutayba calls stone, image or Satan both jibt and taghut, and Ibn al-Jawzi reports al-Zajjaj's Arabic-speaker definition. Qurṭubi adds soothsayers and callers to error; Raghib, reported by Tabatabai, includes transgressors and notes singular or plural use with 2:256, 39:17, 2:257. Baydawi says false deity or tyrant."}, {"id": "16:36/q06/p2", "position": "Satan and whoever calls people to error, or every call toward error.", "reasons": "Wahidi's two commentaries, Tabrisi, Bursevi and Alusi extend the referent from Satan to other misleading callers; Bursevi and Alusi say anything that calls toward error."}, {"id": "16:36/q06/p3", "position": "Satan specifically; avoiding him means refusing his call and obedience.", "reasons": "Yahya cites 4:117 and says Satan called people to idol worship; Tabari stresses fear of his diversion from God's path; Razi reports avoidance of obedience to Satan; Alusi reports al-Hasan's gloss."}, {"id": "16:36/q06/p4", "position": "Idols or false gods specifically.", "reasons": "Yahya reports al-Suddi's alternative to Satan; Ibn al-Jawzi reports a Quranic use for idols; Ibn Ashur calls it a generic term for idols and notes the plural tawaghit with 4:51; Kuranyolu renders it false gods, citing 5:60."}]}
{"id": "16:36/q07", "question": "What is the derivation and form of taghut?", "turns_on": "These are complementary accounts of sense and morphological formation.", "positions": [{"id": "16:36/q07/p1", "position": "It derives from transgression or exceeding bounds and can denote a transgressing human or jinn as well as a false object of worship.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi derives it from tughyān and lists unbeliever, sorcerer, idol, Satan, rebellious jinn or human; Tabatabai reports Raghib's 'any transgressor or object worshipped besides God,' tracing it to unjust excess."}, {"id": "16:36/q07/p2", "position": "It follows the fa'alut pattern, with metathesis and an added nonfeminine ta.", "reasons": "Bursevi compares jabarut and malakut, derives the source form as ṭugh-yut, moves the lam before the ayn, and says the extra ta is not feminine."}]}
{"id": "16:36/q08", "question": "How is the contrasted division among the communities construed?", "turns_on": "The notes offer a semantic division and two permitted grammatical parses of man, rather than rival accounts of who is divided.", "positions": [{"id": "16:36/q08/p1", "position": "After messengers delivered their charge, the nations divided into guided and erring groups.", "reasons": "Bursevi takes minhum back to the nations and the fa as implying that consequence. {"id": "16:36/q10", "question": "What does haqqat mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "16:36/q10/p1", "position": "It became due, binding, established, or inevitable.", "reasons": "Jishumi compares a judgment becoming due and cites 5:107 for liability; Asad gives the literal senses 'error inevitably established' or a verdict of error made inevitable."}]}
